questions.stem:
During design development of a one-story corporate office building, the project architect is checking the code analysis before the 50% DD review. The floor will have open offices and a large conference room furnished with tables and chairs. The jurisdiction has adopted the IBC 2021.

| Area | Size | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Offices and support | 18,000 gross sf | Business |
| Conference room | 2,400 net sf | Assembly, tables and chairs |

What is the design occupant load for the floor?

options.explanation: This counts the business area only and leaves out the conference room.
This uses the older 100 gross sf factor for business areas.
This uses the concentrated-assembly factor (7 net sf) for a room with tables.

questions.explanation:
1. Business: 18,000 ÷ 150 gross = 120
2. Assembly, unconcentrated: 2,400 ÷ 15 net = 160
3. Total = 280 (2 exits required for 1–500)

questions.stem:
A firm is starting schematic design for a medical office building in a city that has adopted the IBC 2021 with local amendments. A designer points out that a newer edition of the IBC has been published and suggests designing to it so the project is current. The city hasn't announced plans to adopt the newer edition before the permit application next year.

Which code should the design follow?

options.text: The newer model code edition, since it is current
options.explanation: A model code isn't law until the jurisdiction adopts it.

options.text: The IBC 2021 as adopted and amended by the city
options.explanation: Correct. The edition and amendments the jurisdiction has adopted govern.

options.text: Whichever edition is less restrictive for each item
options.explanation: Mixing editions to pick the easier provisions isn't allowed.

options.text: The IBC 2021 without the local amendments
options.explanation: Local amendments are part of the adopted code.

questions.explanation: Design to the code the jurisdiction has adopted, including its amendments.

questions.stem:
A developer wants a 6-story office building on an urban site. The zoning ordinance permits buildings up to 75 ft tall on the site. Based on the construction type the developer has selected for cost reasons and the sprinkler system, the IBC 2021 as adopted limits the building to 65 ft above grade plane.

What is the maximum building height the architect can design to?

options.text: 75 ft, because zoning sets the height limit
options.explanation: Zoning is only one limit. The building code also limits height.

options.text: 65 ft, because both limits must be met
options.explanation: Correct. The project must comply with both, so the more restrictive limit controls.

options.text: 70 ft, the average of the two limits
options.explanation: Limits aren't averaged.

options.text: 75 ft, if the building official approves
options.explanation: The building official can't waive a code height limit simply because zoning allows more.

questions.explanation: Zoning and the building code both apply. The more restrictive limit controls.

questions.stem:
An architect is preparing the code analysis for a new apartment building that will first be occupied in 2028. The project's key data is shown below. Each ground-floor unit is reached from a building entrance on an accessible route.

| Item | Data |
|---|---|
| Stories | 3 |
| Units | 24 (8 per floor) |
| Elevator | None |
| Funding | Private |

How many units must meet the Fair Housing Act design requirements?

options.text: 0, because the building has no elevator
options.explanation: Buildings of 4 or more units without an elevator still have covered ground-floor units.

options.text: 8, the ground-floor units
options.explanation: Correct. Without an elevator, the ground-floor units in a building of 4 or more units are covered.

options.text: 12, half of the units
options.explanation: The Act doesn't use a percentage.

options.text: 24, every unit in the building
options.explanation: All units are covered only when the building has an elevator.

questions.explanation: FHA covered multifamily dwellings: with an elevator, all units; without one, ground-floor units (4+ unit buildings).

questions.stem:
A building department returned a firm's last permit submittal because the code analysis was incomplete. For the next project, a three-story mixed-use building, the principal asks the project architect to confirm the code summary sheet will be complete for plan review.

Which items should the code summary include? Check the four that apply.

options.text: Occupancy classification of each space
options.explanation: Correct. Occupancy drives most other code requirements.

options.text: Construction type and fire-resistance ratings
options.explanation: Correct. Construction type sets ratings for the building elements.

options.text: Allowable height and area calculation
options.explanation: Correct. Reviewers check that the building fits the allowable height and area.

options.text: Occupant loads and egress capacity
options.explanation: Correct. Egress depends on occupant loads.

options.text: The contractor's sequence of construction
options.explanation: Sequencing is the contractor's means and methods, not part of the code analysis.

options.text: The owner's projected operating costs
options.explanation: Operating costs aren't a code item.

questions.explanation: Code summary: occupancy, construction type, height and area, occupant load and egress, sprinklers, accessibility.

questions.stem:
A county is building a new public library with county funds. The project architect asks which part of the Americans with Disabilities Act will govern accessibility for the building's design. Construction documents will be submitted for permit next spring.

Which ADA title applies to the library's design?

options.text: Title I, covering employment
options.explanation: Title I covers employment practices, not facility design.

options.text: Title II, covering state and local governments
options.explanation: Correct. A county facility is covered by Title II. New construction must meet the 2010 Standards (28 CFR 35.151).

options.text: Title III, covering public accommodations
options.explanation: Title III covers private entities, not county facilities.

options.text: None, because public buildings follow only the local code
options.explanation: Federal law applies alongside the local code.

questions.explanation: ADA Title II: state and local government facilities (28 CFR 35.151).

questions.stem:
A city plans to renovate a 1920s school listed on the National Register of Historic Places into a community center. Part of the funding is a federal grant. The city wants to start construction documents now, and asks the architect whether any federal review is needed before the grant is approved.

What review must the federal agency complete before approving the grant?

options.text: A Section 106 review of effects on the building
options.explanation: Correct. NHPA Section 106 requires the federal agency to consider effects on historic properties before approving federal funds.

options.text: A Davis-Bacon review of the architect's fees
options.explanation: Davis-Bacon concerns construction wages, not the agency's historic review.

options.text: An accessibility plan review by the U.S. Department of Justice
options.explanation: The DOJ doesn't review plans before construction.

options.text: No review, since the city owns the building
options.explanation: Federal funding triggers the review whoever owns the building.

questions.explanation: Federal funding or permits affecting historic property trigger Section 106 review (54 U.S.C. §306108).

questions.stem:
An owner and contractor have signed an A101-2017 agreement with the A201-2017 general conditions for a new fire station. The contract documents don't say who will obtain the building permit. Plan review is complete, and the permit is ready to be issued. The owner asks the architect who should get it.

Who is responsible for obtaining the building permit?

options.text: The architect, as the design professional of record
options.explanation: The architect assists with filings, but A201 assigns securing the permit to the contractor.

options.text: The contractor, unless the documents say otherwise
options.explanation: Correct. A201-2017 §3.7.1 makes the contractor secure and pay for the building permit by default.

options.text: The owner, as the property owner
options.explanation: The owner may be the applicant in some jurisdictions, but A201's default is the contractor.

options.text: The building official, once the plan review is complete
options.explanation: The building official issues the permit but doesn't obtain it for a party.

questions.explanation: A201-2017 §3.7.1: the contractor secures the building permit unless the documents say otherwise.

flashcards.back: II: state and local government (28 CFR 35.151). III: public accommodations and commercial facilities (28 CFR 36.406).
